qs.q: Binocular vision is typically established by which age range?
qs.e: Binocular vision is established by 3–6 months. A squint is normal before this period, but a persistent or fixed squint requires referral.
qs.s: Normal Development: Milestones from Birth to Five Years: MCQs

qs.q: Which vision assessment is performed at school entry during a well‑child visit?
qs.e: Visual acuity is checked at school entry to detect refractive errors. The red reflex is screened in newborns, not at school age.
qs.s: Evaluation of the Well Child: Surveillance, Screening, Immunisation: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus develops acute changes in mental status, headaches, seizures, and vision loss. Magnetic resonance imaging shows white matter changes in the bilateral parieto-occipital areas due to fluid extravasation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Mononeuritis multiplex of the central nervous system
qs.e: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) presents with acute mental status changes, headaches, seizures, and bilateral parieto-occipital white matter changes on MRI driven by fluid extravasation from sudden blood pressure spikes or medications. Libman-Sacks endocarditis involves cardiac valvular vegetation rather than isolated bilateral occipital white matter edema.

qs.q: A patient with suspected chronic lymphocytic leukaemia presents with headache and blurred vision. What is the investigation of choice to assess for malignant cell infiltration of the central nervous system?
o: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains
qs.e: Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid cytology allows direct assessment for malignant cell infiltration in central nervous system involvement. Imaging modalities like MRI do not provide definitive cellular confirmation of malignant infiltration.
qs.s: Acute Leukaemia (AML/ALL) & WBC Disorders: Haematology Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A patient experiences subacute bilateral loss of central vision due to an inherited defect in oxidative phosphorylation enzymes. Molecular analysis confirms a point mutation in mitochondrial DNA. What condition does this represent?
qs.e: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is caused by mutations in mitochondrial genes encoding oxidative phosphorylation enzymes. Duchenne muscular dystrophy and Huntington disease are nuclear DNA disorders.
qs.s: Genetics & Disease: Muscular Dystrophy, CF, Marfan, Diabetes, Cancer: MCQs

qs.q: Which vitamin deficiency resulting from malabsorption presents with follicular hyperkeratosis and poor night vision?
o: Vitamin B1 deficiency causing neurological deficits
Vitamin C deficiency causing bleeding disorders
Vitamin A deficiency causing night vision issues
Vitamin E deficiency causing posterior column signs
qs.e: Vitamin A deficiency leads to follicular hyperkeratosis and night blindness due to impaired retinal function. Vitamin B1 deficiency causes beriberi, which manifests differently with neurological and cardiovascular signs.

qs.q: A patient with systemic sclerosis develops an abrupt onset of severe headache, blurred vision, and rapidly progressive oliguric renal failure with fragmented RBCs on urinalysis. What is the key initial intervention to improve prognosis?
o: Surgical repair of underlying renal artery stenosis lesions
Immediate high-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy initiation
Initiation of chronic renal replacement therapy via hemodialysis
Prompt administration of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
qs.e: Hypertensive renal crisis requires the prompt use of ACE inhibitors to control blood pressure before irreversible renal failure ensues. Steroid use is actually a risk factor that can precipitate renal crisis.

qs.q: A patient diagnosed with systemic sclerosis develops an abrupt onset of severe headache, blurred vision, and rapidly progressive oliguric renal failure. Urinalysis shows proteinuria, microscopic hematuria, and fragmented RBCs. What is the most critical immediate intervention to improve prognosis in this life-threatening complication?
o: Emergency total thyroidectomy to reduce metabolic demand
Prophylactic administration of broad-spectrum oral antibiotics
Immediate initiation of high-dose intravenous corticosteroids
Prompt use of ACE inhibitors to control blood pressure
qs.e: Hypertensive renal crisis requires the prompt use of ACE inhibitors to bring blood pressure under control before renal failure becomes permanent. High-dose corticosteroids are actually a recognized risk factor that can precipitate renal crisis.

es.q: Describe the screening protocols for vision, hearing, and developmental milestones during well-child visits.
es.m:
- **Vision screening:** Perform a newborn red reflex test, corneal light reflex and cover test for squint, visual acuity at school entry, and refer any squint persisting after 3–4 months.
- **Hearing screening:** Conduct newborn screening where available using otoacoustic emissions, ask about sound responses, and test children with speech delays or risk factors.
- **Developmental surveillance:** Assess development at every visit.
- **Formal developmental tools:** Use a formal tool at 9, 18, and 24–30 months.
- **Autism screening:** Screen using the M-CHAT-R/F tool at 18 and 24 months.
es.s: Evaluation of the Well Child: Surveillance, Screening, Immunisation: Essay quest

es.q: An HIV-positive patient develops progressive vision loss due to retinitis. A newborn presents with microcephaly, brain calcification, and hepatosplenomegaly. 1. Identify the common viral pathogen responsible for both clinical scenarios. 2. What is the characteristic histological finding in infected
es.m: 1. Cytomegalovirus (CMV). 2. Histology/cytology shows multinucleated giant cells with characteristic "owl's eye" intranuclear inclusion bodies. 3. Transplacental, infected birth canal (perinatal), or breastfeeding.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Vision is the process by which light reflected from objects in the environment is detected by the eyes and converted into electrical signals, allowing the brain to form a perception of the world. It involves complex interactions between the eye's structures and neural pathways. Understanding vision is crucial for diagnosing and managing ocular and neurological conditions.

sections.p: Vision is a primary sensory modality that provides detailed information about the external environment. It begins with light entering the eye and being focused onto the retina, where photoreceptor cells convert light energy into neural signals. These signals are then transmitted via the optic nerve to the brain for processing and interpretation, resulting in the perception of images, colors, and motion.
b: Light enters the eye through the cornea and pupil.
The lens focuses light onto the retina at the back of the eye.
Photoreceptors (rods and cones) in the retina detect light.
Neural signals are sent to the brain via the optic nerve.

sections.p: The process of vision involves several key steps, starting with the physical properties of light and culminating in neural processing. Light rays pass through the transparent structures of the eye, which refract and focus them precisely onto the retina. Within the retina, specialized cells initiate the conversion of light into electrical impulses, which are then relayed through a complex neural network to the visual cortex in the brain.
b: Light refraction: Cornea and lens bend light to focus it on the retina.
Accommodation: The lens changes shape to focus on objects at different distances.
Phototransduction: Rods (for dim light, black/white) and cones (for bright light, color) convert light into electrical signals.
Retinal processing: Bipolar, horizontal, amacrine, and ganglion cells process and transmit signals.
Optic nerve: Ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve, carrying signals to the brain.
Visual pathway: Signals travel through the optic chiasm, lateral geniculate nucleus, and optic radiations to the visual cortex.

Central vs. Peripheral Vision: Central vision (macula/fovea) provides high acuity and color perception. Peripheral vision is less sensitive to movement but detects motion and objects outside the direct line of sight.

sections.p: Vision is regulated by both intrinsic ocular mechanisms and extrinsic neural control. The pupil's size, controlled by the autonomic nervous system, regulates the amount of light entering the eye. The ciliary muscles adjust the lens curvature for accommodation, ensuring clear focus. Neural feedback loops within the retina and brain fine-tune visual processing based on environmental conditions and attention.
b: Pupillary light reflex: Autonomic nervous system constricts pupils in bright light, dilates in dim light.
Accommodation reflex: Ciliary muscles adjust lens shape for near or far vision.
Retinal adaptation: Photoreceptors adjust sensitivity to light levels (light and dark adaptation).
Visual attention: Higher brain centers can modulate visual processing to focus on specific stimuli.

sections.p: Disruptions at any point in the visual pathway can lead to impaired vision or blindness. Problems can arise from structural damage to the eye, dysfunction of photoreceptors, or damage to the neural pathways transmitting signals to the brain. Common issues include refractive errors, cataracts, glaucoma, and conditions affecting the retina or optic nerve.
b: Refractive errors: Myopia (nearsightedness), hyperopia (farsightedness), astigmatism (irregular corneal shape).
Cataracts: Clouding of the lens, common in older adults and can be accelerated by diabetes or trauma.
Glaucoma: Damage to the optic nerve, often due to increased intraocular pressure, leading to peripheral vision loss.
Retinopathy: Damage to retinal blood vessels (e.g., diabetic retinopathy, hypertensive retinopathy).
Macular degeneration: Degeneration of the macula, leading to central vision loss, common in the elderly.
Optic neuritis: Inflammation of the optic nerve, causing pain and vision loss, often associated with multiple sclerosis or infections.
Cortical blindness: Damage to the visual cortex in the brain, where the eyes are healthy but the brain cannot process visual information.
Infections: Trachoma (Chlamydia trachomatis) can cause blindness, especially in low-resource settings; herpes simplex virus can cause corneal ulcers.
Nutritional deficiencies: Vitamin A deficiency can lead to night blindness and xerophthalmia, a significant cause of blindness in children in low-resource settings.
Toxic effects: Ethambutol (used for TB) can cause optic neuritis and color vision loss; blocking muscarinic receptors (e.g., with atropine) causes blurred vision.

sections.p: Understanding vision physiology is fundamental for diagnosing and managing a wide range of ocular and systemic diseases. Clinicians assess visual acuity, visual fields, and ocular structures to pinpoint the location and nature of visual impairments. Early detection and intervention are crucial for preserving vision and preventing irreversible damage, especially in conditions like glaucoma or diabetic retinopathy.
b: Visual acuity testing: Measures the sharpness of vision (e.g., Snellen chart).
Visual field testing: Assesses peripheral vision and detects defects caused by glaucoma or neurological lesions.
Fundoscopy: Examination of the retina, optic disc, and retinal blood vessels for signs of disease.
Intraocular pressure measurement: Screens for glaucoma.
Pupillary light reflex assessment: Indicates optic nerve or brainstem function.

Developmental screening: Assessing fine motor and vision milestones (reaching, grasping, transferring objects) is critical in children to detect developmental delays or concerns about vision or hearing.
Danger signs in pregnancy: Blurred vision can indicate pre-eclampsia, requiring urgent medical attention.

t.b: Measures visual acuity. A result of 20/20 (or 6/6) means normal vision; higher numbers (e.g., 20/200) indicate poorer vision.

Examines the retina, optic disc, and blood vessels. Abnormalities like optic disc cupping (glaucoma), hemorrhages (diabetic retinopathy), or papilledema (increased intracranial pressure) indicate specific pathologies. If unavailable, a red reflex test can screen for significant opacities like cataracts in children.
Measures intraocular pressure. Elevated pressure (e.g., >21 mmHg) is a risk factor for glaucoma, though normal tension glaucoma exists.

Assesses the extent of peripheral vision. Defects (e.g., scotomas, hemianopia) localize lesions in the visual pathway. If formal perimetry is unavailable, a confrontation test can provide a quick, albeit less precise, assessment.

sections.p: For exams, focus on the entire visual pathway from light entry to cortical processing. Be able to trace the path of light and neural signals, identify the function of each structure, and explain how common pathologies disrupt this process. Pay attention to the clinical manifestations of lesions at different points in the pathway.
b: Remember the difference between rods (dim light, peripheral vision) and cones (bright light, color, central vision).
Understand the pupillary light reflex pathway and its clinical significance.
Know the visual field defects associated with lesions at different points along the optic pathway (e.g., optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract).
Be able to explain the mechanism of accommodation and why it declines with age (presbyopia).
Connect systemic diseases (diabetes, hypertension) to their ocular manifestations (retinopathy).

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes
Sudden onset of blurred vision or double vision
Seeing flashes of light or new floaters
Persistent severe headache with blurred vision
Any concerns about a child's vision or developmental milestones related to vision

faq.q: Why do I see better in the dark after a while?
faq.a: This is dark adaptation. Your rods, which are more sensitive to dim light, gradually become more active and regenerate their photopigment, increasing your overall sensitivity to light.
Color blindness is usually a genetic condition where one or more types of cone photoreceptors in the retina are absent or dysfunctional, most commonly affecting red-green perception.

faq.q: Why do some medications cause blurred vision?
faq.a: Some medications, like anticholinergics, can block muscarinic receptors, paralyzing the ciliary muscle and preventing accommodation, leading to blurred near vision. Others, like ethambutol, can damage the optic nerve.
